title: Search, Ranking, and Information Retrieval
learning_outcomes: Explain search, Ranking, and Information Retrieval and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in search, Ranking, and Information Retrieval to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study search, Ranking, and Information Retrieval within Specialized Fields of Artificial Intelligence. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: AI specializations reuse shared foundations but differ in data, output, evaluation, and deployment constraints. Choose a method for a defined use case.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Retrieval identifies candidate information and ranking orders it for a query or goal. Measure whether relevant items are retrieved before measuring how well they are ranked, and monitor relevance, diversity, and latency.

items.text: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant evidence and supplies it to a generator. Evaluate retrieval coverage, source relevance, grounding, and abstention separately; adding a retrieval step does not guarantee a supported answer.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what search, ranking, and information retrieval takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. AI specializations reuse shared foundations but differ in data, output, evaluation, and deployment constraints. Choose a method for a defined use case.

content_blocks.code:
documents = {"doc-1": "refund policy", "doc-2": "shipping times", "doc-3": "refund window"}
query = "refund"
results = [doc_id for doc_id, text in documents.items() if query in text]
print("matching documents:", results)
content_blocks.run_instructions: Copy the code into a local file named main.py and run `python main.py` with Python 3. Compare the printed output with the expected result documented here. This CodeLeaf content block is static; it does not execute the snippet in the browser and needs no external API key.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content.task: Try it yourself: choose a small, synthetic example for search, ranking, and information retrieval. Explain the inputs and outputs, compare a simple baseline where appropriate, and write one limitation that should be checked on representative data.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
